claim.text: The implicit mirror potential induced by the overparameterization $x=m\odot w$ with initialization satisfying $m_{0,i} > |w_{0,i}|$ for all $i\in[n]$ equals $$ R(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\,\operatorname{arcsinh}\!\left(\frac{x_i}{2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}}\right)\;-\;\sqrt{x_i^2+4u_{0,i}^2v_{0,i}^2}\;-\;x_i\log\!\left(\frac{u_{0,i}}{v_{0,i}}\right), $$ where $u_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}+w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $v_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}-w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$.
The function $R$, the implicit mirror potential induced by the overparameterization $x=m\odot w$, is a Bregman potential.

The smoothness (Lipschitz constant of its gradient inverse) of the function $R$, the implicit mirror potential induced by the overparameterization $x=m\odot w$, depends on the initialization via the factor $2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}$, where $u_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}+w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $v_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}-w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$.

For the mirror potential $R(x)=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(x_i\operatorname{arcsinh}\!\left(\frac{x_i}{a}\right)-\sqrt{x_i^2+a^2}-x_i\log\!\left(\frac{u_{0,i}}{v_{0,i}}\right)\right)$ (the corrected hyperbolic-entropy variant), where $u_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}+w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$, $v_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}-w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$, and $2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}=a$ for all $i$, in the regime $a\to 0$ and $|x_i/a|\to\infty$ one has $$ R(x)\sim \log\!\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)\,||x||_{L_1}. $$
Obtaining the $L_1$-dominant regime described in claim 4 requires $a$ to be exponentially small relative to relevant magnitudes.
As described in claim 5, this makes zero or near-zero initializations numerically problematic and potentially causes saddle-point slowdowns.

For underdetermined linear regression problems $f(x)=\tilde f(Zx-Y)$ with $n>d$, if $f$ is quasi-convex, $\nabla f$ is locally Lipschitz, and $\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)$ is non-empty, then gradient flow on the overparameterized variables $(m,w)$ (with $x=m\odot w$) converges to a limit $x^*$ that solves $$ x^* \;=\; \operatorname{argmin}_{Zx=Y} R(x), $$

Adding weight decay regularization $h(m,w)=\sum_{i=1}^n(m_i^2+w_i^2)$ with time-varying coefficient $\alpha_t\ge 0$ to gradient flow on $(m,w)$ yields a time-dependent mirror potential governing the dynamics in $x=m\odot w$: $$ R_{a_t}(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\,\operatorname{arcsinh}\!\left(\frac{x_i}{a_{t,i}}\right) - \sqrt{x_i^2 + a_{t,i}^2} - x_i\log\!\left(\frac{u_{0,i}}{v_{0,i}}\right), $$ for $a_{t,i}=2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}\exp\!\big(-2\int_0^t\alpha_s ds\big)$ with $u_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}+w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $v_{0,i}=\frac{m_{0,i}-w_{0,i}}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The dynamics in $x=m\odot w$ arising from adding weight decay regularization $h(m,w)=\sum_{i=1}^n(m_i^2+w_i^2)$ with time-varying coefficient $\alpha_t\ge 0$ to gradient flow on $(m,w)$, governed by the time-dependent mirror potential $R_{a_t}(x)$ described in claim 9, satisfy the time-dependent mirror-flow identity $$ d\!\big(\nabla R_{a_t}(x_t)\big) \;=\; -\nabla f(x_t)\,dt,\qquad x_0=m_0\odot w_0. $$

A decaying schedule for the time-varying weight decay coefficient $\alpha_t\ge 0$ (as described in claim 9) directly controls the scale $a_t$, where $a_{t,i}=2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}\exp\!\big(-2\int_0^t\alpha_s ds\big)$, of the mirror potential $R_{a_t}(x)$ governing the dynamics that satisfy $d\!\big(\nabla R_{a_t}(x_t)\big) = -\nabla f(x_t)\,dt$ (as described in claim 9, claim 10), and thereby the strength and position of the implicit bias.

Given $\alpha_t\ge 0$ satisfying $\int_0^\infty \alpha_s ds<\infty$, and assuming $f$ is quasi-convex or satisfies the PL inequality with constant $\lambda>0$, and considering the time-dependent Bregman potential $R_{a_t}$ as given in note 1, the time-dependent mirror flow $d\nabla R_{a_t}(x_t)=-\nabla f(x_t)dt$ converges to a critical point $x^*$.
If $f$ is convex or satisfies PL then $x^*$, the critical point to which the time-dependent mirror flow converges as stated in claim 12, is an interpolating minimizer of $f$.

In the PL case, where $f$ satisfies the PL inequality with constant $\lambda>0$, the loss along the time-dependent mirror flow $d\nabla R_{a_t}(x_t)=-\nabla f(x_t)dt$ satisfies the finite-time bound $$ f(x_t)-f(x^*) \le B\exp\!\big(-\lambda a_\infty t\big), $$ where $a_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}a_t$ and $$ B=(f(x_0)-f(x^*))\exp\!\Big(C||x^*||_{L_2}\!\int_0^\infty\alpha_s ds\Big), $$ with $C$ a constant depending on the smoothness of $f$.

For underdetermined linear regression $f(x)=\tilde f(Zx-Y)$, under the conditions that $f$ quasi-convex, $\nabla f$ locally Lipschitz, $\operatorname{argmin} f$ non-empty, $\alpha_t\ge 0$, $\int_0^\infty\alpha_sds<\infty$, the limit $x^*$ of the time-dependent mirror flow satisfies $$ x^* \;=\; \operatorname{argmin}_{Zx=Y} R_{a_\infty}(x), $$ where $R_{a_\infty}$ is the Bregman potential $R_{a_t}$ in the limit $t\to\infty$ with $a_\infty = \lim_{t\to\infty} a_{t,i}$.

This combination of parameterizing weights as $x=m\odot w$, applying weight decay $h(m,w)=\sum_i(m_i^2+w_i^2)$ with a time-dependent coefficient $\alpha_t$, and using an initialization that fixes the per-coordinate scale $2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}$ to a chosen constant across parameters yields a time-dependent Bregman potential $R_{a_t}$ that can be driven towards an $L_1$-like regime (where it approximates the $L_1$ norm) without requiring zero initialization, thereby providing a tunable implicit $L_1$-regularization while preserving convergence of the loss and the optimal interpolator selection property for underdetermined linear regression (the limit minimizes $R_{a_\infty}$ among interpolators).

In simulated diagonal linear networks for underdetermined sparse recovery ($d=40$, $n=100$, ground-truth $||x^*||_{L_0}=5$), the proposed PILoT initialization (constant per-coordinate scale $2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}=1$) together with a strongly decaying $\alpha_t$ schedule recovers the ground-truth $x^*$ faster and more accurately (smaller $||x_t-x^*||_{L_2}$ trajectories) than baselines.

In simulated diagonal linear networks for underdetermined sparse recovery ($d=40$, $n=100$, ground-truth $||x^*||_{L_0}=5$), Spred initialization with $2u_{0}v_{0}=0$ fails to approach the ground truth $x^*$ for all regularization strengths tested.

In one-shot pruning experiments (train for 150 epochs, then remove smallest weights) on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the $m\odot w$ parameterization with PILoT regularization achieves higher validation accuracy than standard baselines and alternative continuous parameterizations across sparsity levels and is particularly robust in the high-sparsity regime.
Simple $L_1$ on $x$ can perform well at some settings.
Simple $L_1$ on $x$ is less robust to regularization strength and degrades more severely at extreme sparsities than PILoT.

When combined with iterative pruning protocols (Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) and Learning Rate Rewinding (LRR)) on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, training the networks with the $m\odot w$ parameterization and PILoT regularization produces higher final accuracies at high sparsity compared to the same iterative schemes using the standard parameterization.
Learning Rate Rewinding (LRR) with PILoT identifies the sparsest winning tickets.
Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with PILoT becomes competitive with Learning Rate Rewinding (LRR), outperforming Learning Rate Rewinding (LRR) at some sparsity levels.
Weight decay applied symmetrically to both $m$ and $w$ commutes with the $m\odot w$ parameterization.
Weight decay applied symmetrically to both $m$ and $w$ is necessary to obtain the derived time-dependent mirror-flow description.
Regularizing only $m$ does not satisfy the necessary Lie-bracket commutation condition (that the Lie bracket span of the gradient vector fields is in the kernel of the Jacobian).

Neuronwise mask parameterizations (mask per neuron instead of per parameter) violate the same Lie-bracket condition (that the Lie bracket span of the gradient vector fields is in the kernel of the Jacobian).
Neuronwise mask parameterizations (mask per neuron instead of per parameter) do not induce a mirror-flow implicit bias of the same form.

In simulated diagonal linear networks for underdetermined sparse recovery ($d=40$, $n=100$, ground-truth $||x^*||_{L_0}=5$), the proposed PILoT initialization (constant per-coordinate scale $2u_{0,i}v_{0,i}=1$) together with a strongly decaying $\alpha_t$ schedule recovers the ground-truth $x^*$ faster and more accurately (smaller $||x_t-x^*||_{L_2}$ trajectories) than the baselines of spred initialization, $L_1$ on $m$ only, and standard $L_1$ on $x$.
